item.title: Aoun accuses Israel of refusing to implement agreement
item.description:
Aoun accuses Israel of refusing to implement agreement

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has called for diplomacy to resolve the conflict with Israel during talks with European Commission Vice President Kaja Kallas in Beirut.

His office quoted him as saying that “negotiation is an alternative to war and agreement is the only means to end the state of hostility between Lebanon and Israel”.

Aoun said the Lebanese army “is fully performing its duty in the areas where it is deployed south of the Litani in implementation of the ‘Framework Agreement,’ while Israel still refuses to implement its provisions”.

He also emphasised the “interconnection between Lebanon’s stability and the stability of Europe and the region”.

According to the presidency, Kallas said the EU “is ready to provide the necessary assistance to Lebanon, especially to the army, the Internal Security Forces and the entities concerned with social and humanitarian aspects”.

The precarious ceasefire halted the fiercest fighting between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah. Israel continues to violate the truce and occupy parts of southern Lebanon.

item.title: How Gulf states are refinancing sovereign wealth funds as Iran war hits revenues
item.description:
How Gulf states are refinancing sovereign wealth funds as Iran war hits revenues

Submitted by Ahmed Alqarout on Wed, 09/30/2026 - 17:27
A small group of US and Canadian firms now sit across Gulf energy infrastructure and money, as the boundaries between sovereign wealth and private capital are breaking down
The logo for Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund is pictured during an event in Indian Wells, California, on 13 March 2024 (Matthew Stockman/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

Four Gulf states have rewritten the mandates of their main sovereign wealth funds since January. Officials have presented each change as long-planned institutional maturity. 

Not one has mentioned the Iran war, but wartime financial pressure signals the changes are being driven by fiscal recalculations as well. 

The restructuring accelerates a prewar trend. Since October 2023, Gulf funds have been cutting back spending and shifting towards narrower revenue-generating activities, as global geopolitical turmoil has driven up costs.

In July, the state-owned Kuwait Oil Company put its crude pipeline network into a joint venture with US investment funds Blackstone and KKR, and Canada's Brookfield. The $16bn deal left the Kuwaiti side holding a 51 percent stake and leasing 13 pipelines back for 20.5 years, in exchange for a volume-based tariff. Kuwait took $7.85bn upfront.

Kuwait spent the rest of the year building the law around deals like this, with new economic courts, an amended capital markets statute, and a plan to rewrite a quarter of its legislation by December. 

A few weeks ago, Kuwait issued a decree to let the treasury borrow from the Future Generations Fund, the pot set aside for the generation after oil. The 1976 law that created it had banned withdrawals outright. 

Borrowing is now capped at a tenth of the fund’s net assets, recorded as a debt owed back and repayable once the budget returns to surplus.

Engine of growth

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, ran a deficit of 160 billion riyals ($42.6bn) in the first half of the year - its worst since 2016. The Public Investment Fund (PIF) was once filled by the state from oil receipts, but there is less to give now, so it raises its own funding. 

The PIF sold $2bn of sukuk, a type of financial certificate, in January, and a record $7bn of bonds in May, for which investors bid around $29bn. The money ultimately goes into companies owned by the PIF, which return some of it as dividends and taxes to state coffers.

The pressure is not expected to ease. The ministry's pre-budget statement for 2027 projects a deficit of 190 billion riyals ($50bn), around 3.6 percent of GDP, to be met by further borrowing and by what it calls alternative financing through project finance, infrastructure finance and export credit agencies.

The PIF recently ordered spending cuts across more than 100 of its companies, slowing projects and laying people off, months before the board approved its 2026-30 plan this past April, splitting the fund into three portfolios named Vision, Strategic and Financial. The plan describes the fund moving from being the primary engine of growth to the steward of platforms that let others scale, while it facilitates borrowing and foreign investment.

The funds are betting that the new borrowing will at least push the financial strain temporarily away, while new investment revenues come in before outstanding bills are due

In September, PIF executives reportedly flew to New York with representatives from the AI firm Humain, the King Abdullah Financial District, and real-estate developer Red Sea Global, where they were set to meet investors from mega funds Apollo, Blackstone, Brookfield, Carlyle, KKR, Stonepeak and the US Export-Import Bank. 

The Saudis were reportedly looking for foreign backing amid cash constraints at home. Three of those firms had bought Kuwait’s pipelines two months earlier.

For Qatar, companies at home are losing their earning power, and a fund that holds them is more expensive to borrow against. On 20 September, the prime minister carved roughly one-third out of the $580bn sovereign fund into a platform called Doha Investment, holding more than 40 companies, including Qatar Airways and Qatar National Bank. 

Its job is to back national champions, deepen capital markets and bring in international capital. It opened with a $60bn pipeline of opportunities, with $38.5bn in infrastructure projects, including public-private partnerships.

Separated, each half carries its own risk profile. Lenders and investors now price Doha Investment on its own rather than against the whole fund, which lets Qatar borrow against its strongest assets on better terms and bring partners into the weaker ones.

Boundaries dissolving

Earlier in 2026, Abu Dhabi folded its wealth fund ADQ, worth $263bn, into a new vehicle called L’imad, with $300bn and more than 250 group subsidiary companies. In July, it brought in Boston Consulting Group and started calling itself an operationally active shareholder, rather than an investor. 

Last week, Bloomberg reported that L’imad was preparing to raise money from outside investors for a unit being built to back private equity funds and make its own deals.

The funds have not stopped their outside deals, but refocused them. Earlier in September, the US Federal Communications Commission cleared the way for 49.5 percent foreign ownership of Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros Discovery. Of that, three Gulf funds would hold 38.5 percent of non-voting equity: PIF with 15.1 percent, L’imad with 12.8 and the Qatar Investment Authority with 10.6. The deal has not closed, and litigation could push completion into 2027. 

Has US war on Iran killed the 'Gulf moment'?
Read More »

Days later, Qatar signed a memorandum with JPMorgan Asset Management for a $20bn partnership, $5bn of it lending to mid-sized American firms. JPMorgan then helped to arrange the Qatari state’s own $3bn bond issuance. 

A small group of American and Canadian firms now sit across Gulf energy infrastructure and Gulf money at the same time, lending against assets they will not operate while managing the cash those assets generate. The funds were built to hold what oil earned, and are now being run to earn what oil no longer does, while holding up budgets and state-owned companies.

Slowly, the boundaries between sovereign wealth, fiscal financing and private capital are breaking down. The funds are betting that the new borrowing will at least push the financial strain temporarily away, while new investment revenues come in before outstanding bills are due. 

If so, the Gulf will have financed its transition with other people’s money, kept its savings, and come out with deeper capital markets and companies run to a standard outsiders are willing to pay for.

Yet a struggling global economy may fail to deliver expected results. If revenues and borrowing do not pick up fast enough, these states will have less room to manoeuvre, and Gulf citizens will likely foot the bill in their livelihoods, which may increase social strains. Social spending cuts, higher taxes and an overall decline in quality of life would follow.

item.title: Iranian press review: 80m barrels behind oil minister’s resignation
item.description:
Iranian press review: 80m barrels behind oil minister’s resignation

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Thu, 10/08/2026 - 09:56
Meanwhile, an analyst says US withdrawal from Iraq could disadvantage Iran, tighter western immigration rules push Iranians towards China and Russia, and Armenia emerges as a key trade partner
The Iranian-flagged cargo ship Nora Bandar Abbas docked at the port of Umm Qasr in southern Iraq on 17 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

Minister falls victim to oil brokers network

Local media have linked Iranian Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation on Sunday to growing tensions over the role of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security figures in the national oil industry, as Iran faces difficulties selling its oil amid international sanctions and a US naval blockade.

Local media had previously reported that a group of four oil brokers close to senior IRGC security officials had been tasked with selling 80 million barrels of Iranian oil at discounted prices.

Officials denied the reports, while Paknejad’s resignation was attributed to personal reasons. But on Tuesday, the Saazandegi daily said pressure over the sale of the 80 million barrels was the main reason for his resignation.

According to Saazandegi, tensions arose between Paknejad and President Masoud Pezeshkian during one of the last cabinet meetings the oil minister attended.

'During war, sanctions and blockade, who is going to sell Iran’s oil, and who will oversee the oil brokers?'

- Saazandegi daily

The daily said the "growing power of the oil sales intermediary network", "uncertainty over the collection of oil revenues placed in its hands", and "parliament and oversight bodies becoming involved in investigating the oil brokers' activities" were among the factors that forced Paknejad to resign.

Saazandegi also addressed a question that has increasingly circulated in Iran over the past month: where is the money from the country’s oil sales?

Describing the difficulties Iran faces in selling oil and bringing the proceeds back into the country, the daily said Paknejad’s resignation had created a new problem for the sector.

“Now the question ‘Where is the oil money?’ has given way to a bigger question,” Saazandegi wrote. “During war, sanctions and blockade, who is going to sell Iran’s oil, and who will oversee the oil brokers?"

Meanwhile, Abdolhossein Hemmati Saraparde, deputy head of parliament’s energy commission, told the economic daily Donya-e Eqtesad that parliament was investigating contracts to sell Iranian oil.

He acknowledged that even the oil minister was unaware of the details of some contracts arranged to sell oil to China.

“The investigation and reviews are under way, but it is not yet possible to identify a specific person as responsible or determine the extent of any violations,” Saraparde said.

US exit from Iraq may hurt Iran in short term

Nozar Shafiei, a Tehran University academic, has suggested that the withdrawal of American forces from Iraq could work against Iran’s interests as the war with the US continues.

Iranian press review: Iranian elite profit billions from oil sanctions
Read More »

Shafiei, an international relations analyst, said the US withdrawal had been planned in advance, partly because of the costs of maintaining forces in Iraq and partly because of Iraqi opposition to their presence.

But he argued that the departure of US forces would also remove them from the reach of Iran and Iran-aligned groups in Iraq.

“The presence of these forces was an Achilles’ heel for the US in Iraq and imposed limitations on Washington in dealing with Iran,” Shafiei was quoted as saying by the Etemad newspaper.

According to Shafiei, the withdrawal of US forces could therefore take them out of Iran’s reach in Iraq while also removing American troops from the battlefield.

He concluded that while the withdrawal might benefit Iran in the long term, it could be damaging to it in the short term.

Iranians look east as western migration routes become harder

Iranians are increasingly looking to China and Russia as rising foreign-exchange costs and tighter immigration rules in western countries make traditional destinations harder to access, the Haft-e Sobh daily reported.

China is becoming a growing destination for Iranian students and technical professionals, particularly those with experience working on Chinese projects in Iran.

US sparks criticism after halting student visa appointments and extending ‘social media vetting’
Read More »

Russia is also attracting Iranians, including businesspeople, through its foreign investment programmes. Both countries are offering alternatives as access to western destinations becomes more difficult for Iranian applicants.

The shift is also affecting Iranian students, who in previous years were among the largest groups applying to universities in western countries but are increasingly looking towards China and Russia as established routes become harder to access.

Migration expert Saeed Salari told Haft-e Sobh that nationality plays a significant role in visa and employment applications, with Iranian applicants facing greater scrutiny in western countries.

He said the falling value of Iran’s currency has also made migration unaffordable for many Iranians, pushing those still able to leave toward cheaper and geographically closer destinations.

The daily added that Turkey and Armenia had also gained prominence among Iranians as regional alternatives for migration.

Tehran seeks to expand ties with Yerevan

Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan's visit to Tehran on Monday and his meetings with the Iranian president and foreign minister have fuelled speculation that Iran is seeking to expand overland trade through Armenia.

Can Baghdad gain control over paramilitary groups amid US war on Iran?
Read More »

Iran has faced serious disruptions to imports and exports in recent months due to the US naval blockade, prompting Tehran to turn to road and rail links with neighbouring countries.

On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted a video on Instagram of his meeting with Mirzoyan and said the talks focused on “the expanding relations between Tehran and Yerevan and ways to deepen cooperation in the economic, trade, transport, energy and other areas of interest to the two countries”.

Farsi media have also highlighted the geopolitical and economic importance of Iran’s land border with Armenia amid the US blockade.

The news website Fararu wrote that “relations with Yerevan are not merely a bilateral matter, but part of a policy to preserve Iran’s access to the Caucasus and maintain the importance of its transport routes in the region”.

The meeting also carries significance in the context of the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan. 

Tehran and Yerevan have moved closer as Azerbaijan has expanded its military and intelligence cooperation with Israel in recent years, a development that has contributed to closer ties between the two countries.

*Iranian press review is a digest of news reports not independently verified as accurate by MEE.

item.title: Morning update
item.description:
Morning update

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

Here are the latest developments: 

  • US President Donald Trump said that his special envoy Steve Witkoff is "doing very well" in discussions with Iran, but added that a deal with Tehran is not his preferred outcome. Trump also expressed that he expects the war on Iran to end soon, saying: "That war ends - it's going to be very soon. It's got to be very soon," he said, describing Iran as "a failed nation."

  • Yemen's Ansar Allah (Houthis) said they attacked the King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The group separately said it downed a Saudi drone while it was carrying out what they described as "hostile missions" over Taiz.

  • A White House official said that President Trump will not allow the Iranian government to "manipulate" him as he claimed Tehran did with previous US presidents. The official told Al Jazeera that Trump was "comfortable letting Iran’s inevitable collapse take its course", adding that the US was in a powerful position because it "controlled the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s economy was collapsing".

  • The Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson said that Tehran has "clearly and firmly" set out conditions for ending the war, adding that it will respond to US proposals through mediators. "Our considerations and conditions for ending the imposed war on all fronts and restoring security to the Persian Gulf region and the Strait of Hormuz have been clearly and firmly set out," Esmaeil Baghaei said.

  • Yemen’s government forces say they have “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters in 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions in the “Dawn of Yemen” operation. In a post on X, the military spokesperson said the strikes targeted Houthi movements, fortifications, supply lines and military positions.
